source: MIT 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms, Lecture 1, ~20-28 min
keypoints: With the greater-than-or-equal-to definition of a peak, every array always has a peak (left as a homework argument).
With a strict greater-than definition, you cannot argue that a peak always exists.
Algorithmic thinking means creating general algorithms that still give a starting point when the problem definition changes.
When no peak can be found, the valid answer is an exhaustive-search argument: a proof that you searched everywhere and none exists.
The straightforward one-dimensional peak finder starts from the left and walks across the array.
Worst case for the straightforward algorithm: the peak is at the far right (e.g. 1,2,3,4,5,6), requiring a look at all n elements.
The worst-case complexity of the straightforward algorithm is theta(n), i.e. linear.
Theta(n) gives both a lower bound and an upper bound ('of the order of n'); Big-O(n) is only an upper bound.
The analysis here cares only about asymptotic complexity, ignoring constants.
A faster approach (binary search): look at the middle element and recurse into the half with the higher neighbor, because a peak must exist on that side.
